Introduction to JavaScript

JavaScript (JS) is a high-level, versatile, and widely used programming language primarily known for making websites interactive and dynamic. It was created by Brendan Eich in 1995 while working at Netscape, initially designed to add simple interactivity to web pages. Over time, it has evolved into one of the core technologies of web development, alongside HTML and CSS.

Key Characteristics

  • High-level language: Easy to read and write with human-friendly syntax.
  • Interpreted language: Executes directly in the browser without needing compilation.
  • Event-driven: Perfect for handling user interactions like clicks, form submissions, and animations.
  • Versatile: Runs on both client-side and server-side using environments like Node.js.
  • Object-oriented and functional: Supports both programming paradigms.

Why JavaScript is Important

  • Web Interactivity: Adds animations, form validations, dropdown menus, sliders, and more.
  • Full-Stack Development: With Node.js, developers can use JavaScript for both front-end and back-end.
  • Huge Ecosystem: Includes libraries and frameworks like React, Angular, Vue.js, and Express.js.
  • Cross-Platform: Powers web apps, mobile apps, desktop apps, and even IoT devices.

Common Use Cases

  • Front-End Development – Creating dynamic and responsive user interfaces.
  • Back-End Development – Building APIs and server-side applications with Node.js.
  • Web Animation & Graphics – Using libraries like GSAP or Three.js.
  • Mobile Apps – Developing mobile apps with frameworks like React Native.
  • Game Development – Building browser-based games using Canvas and WebGL.

// Display a greeting in the browser console

//the alert is use to popup the massege in the web page

JavaScript Variables & Data Types

Variables in JavaScript are used to store data that can be used and manipulated throughout your program. JavaScript is dynamically typed, meaning you don't need to explicitly declare the type of a variable — it’s determined at runtime.

1. Declaring Variables

There are three ways to declare variables in JavaScript:

Keyword Scope Reassignment Hoisting Use Case
var Global-scoped Yes Hoisted with undefined Legacy code (avoid in modern JS)
let Block-scoped Yes Hoisted but not initialized For variables that need to change
const Block-scoped No Hoisted but not initialized For variables that should not change 
// Example
var name = "Alice";   // Old way
let age = 25;         // Modern way
const country = "USA"; // Cannot be reassigned

age = 26; // ✅ Works
// country = "Canada"; ❌ Error

2. JavaScript Data Types

JavaScript data types are divided into two main categories:

  • Primitive Data Types: These hold a single value and are immutable.
  • Non-Primitive Data Types: These are mutable and can hold multiple values or complex structures.

Primitive Data Types

  • String - Represents textual data. Example: "Hello"
  • Number - Represents numbers (integer or floating-point). Example: 42
  • Boolean - Represents logical values: true or false
  • Undefined - A variable declared but not assigned a value.
  • Null - Represents intentional absence of any value.
  • Symbol - Represents unique identifiers (ES6).
  • BigInt - Represents very large integers beyond safe limits.
// Primitive Examples
let name = "Alice";         // String
let age = 25;               // Number
let isStudent = true;       // Boolean
let score;                  // Undefined
let emptyValue = null;      // Null
let uniqueId = Symbol("id");// Symbol
let bigNumber = 9007199254740991n; // BigInt

Non-Primitive Data Types

  • Object - Collection of key-value pairs. Example: {name: "John", age: 30}
  • Array - Ordered list of values. Example: [1, 2, 3]
  • Function - A block of code designed to perform a particular task.
// Non-Primitive Examples
let person = { name: "Alice", age: 25 }; // Object
let colors = ["Red", "Green", "Blue"];   // Array
function greet() {                        // Function
  return "Hello!";
}

3. Checking Data Types

Use the typeof operator to check the type of a variable:


console.log(typeof "Hello");   // string
console.log(typeof 42);        // number
console.log(typeof true);      // boolean
console.log(typeof undefined); // undefined
console.log(typeof null);      // object (historical quirk)
console.log(typeof []);        // object
console.log(typeof greet);     // function

Arithmetic Operators

`+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `**`, `++`, `--`
let x = 10, y = 5;
[
  ["x + y", x + y],
  ["x - y", x - y],
  ["x * y", x * y],
  ["x / y", x / y],
  ["x % y", x % y],
  ["x ** 2", x ** 2],
  ["x++ (post)", (t=>{let a=t; t++; return `${a} → ${t}`;})(10)],
  ["++y (pre)", (t=>{let a=t; return `${++a}`;})(5)],
]

Assignment Operators

`=`, `+=`, `-=`, `*=`, `/=`, `%=`
let a = 10;
a += 5;   // 15
a -= 3;   // 12
a *= 2;   // 24
a /= 4;   // 6
a %= 5;   // 1

Comparison Operators

`==`, `===`, `!=`, `!==`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` 
let x = 10; 
[
  ['x == "10"', x == "10"],      // true (coercion)
  ['x === "10"', x === "10"],    // false (strict)
  ['x != 5', x != 5],
  ['x !== 10', x !== 10],
  ['x > 5', x > 5],
  ['x <= 10', x <= 10],
]

Logical Operators

`&&` (AND), `||` (OR), `!` (NOT)
let x = 10, y = 5;
[
  ['x > 5 && y < 10', x > 5 && y < 10],
  ['x > 5 || y > 10', x > 5 || y > 10],
  ['!(x > 5)', !(x > 5)],
]

Ternary Operator

`condition ? exprIfTrue : exprIfFalse`
const age = 18;
const msg = (age >= 18) ? 'You are an adult' : 'You are a minor';
msg; // → 'You are an adult'

Type Operators

`typeof`, `instanceof`
typeof 42;           // 'number'
typeof 'hi';         // 'string'
typeof null;         // 'object' (quirk)
[1,2,3] instanceof Array; // true

Nullish Coalescing

`a ?? b` → returns a unless it is null or undefined 
let user = null;
let name = user ?? 'Guest'; // 'Guest'

let count = 0;
let shown = count ?? 10;    // 0 (because 0 is not null/undefined)

Conditional Statements — if / else if / else

Classic branching based on boolean conditions.
function grade(score) {
  if (score >= 90) return 'A';
  else if (score >= 75) return 'B';
  else if (score >= 60) return 'C';
  else return 'D';
}

grade(85); // 'B'

switch Statement

Choose one of many code paths based on a value.
function dayName(n) {
  switch (n) {
    case 1: return 'Monday';
    case 2: return 'Tuesday';
    case 3: return 'Wednesday';
    case 4: return 'Thursday';
    case 5: return 'Friday';
    case 6: return 'Saturday';
    case 7: return 'Sunday';
    default: return 'Invalid';
  }
}

dayName(3); // 'Wednesday'

Bonus: Optional Chaining

Safely access deep properties: obj?.a?.b
const user = { profile: { name: 'Ava' } };
const good = user?.profile?.name;    // 'Ava'
const safe = user?.address?.street;  // undefined (no error)

JavaScript Loops and String

JavaScript Loops Explained

Loops are used to repeat a block of code multiple times until a certain condition is met. They help programmers avoid writing repetitive code and make programs more efficient. JavaScript offers several types of loops, each serving different purposes.

1. The for Loop

The for loop is used when you know how many times you want to execute a block of code. It consists of three parts:

  • Initialization: Runs once before the loop starts (e.g., let i = 0;).
  • Condition: Checked before each iteration. If true, the loop runs.
  • Increment/Decrement: Runs after each loop iteration (e.g., i++).
// Example: Print numbers 1 to 5
for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  console.log("Number:", i);
}

2. The while Loop

The while loop is used when you do not know beforehand how many times the loop should run. It continues running as long as the condition is true. 

// Example: Print numbers 1 to 5
let i = 1;
while (i <= 5) {
  console.log("Number:", i);
  i++;
}

3. The do...while Loop

The do...while loop is similar to while, but it guarantees that the block of code will run at least once before checking the condition. 

// Example: Print numbers 1 to 5
let i = 1;
do {
  console.log("Number:", i);
  i++;
} while (i <= 5);

4. The for...of Loop

The for...of loop is used to iterate over arrays, strings, and other iterable objects. It is best for when you need values directly. 

// Example: Loop through an array
const colors = ["Red", "Green", "Blue"];
for (let color of colors) {
  console.log("Color:", color);
}

5. The for...in Loop

The for...in loop is used to iterate over the keys (properties) of an object. 

// Example: Loop through an object
const person = { name: "Alice", age: 25, city: "New York" };
for (let key in person) {
  console.log(key + ": " + person[key]);
}

6. forEach() Method

The forEach() method is available on arrays and is used to execute a function once for each array element. 

// Example: Using forEach
const numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];
numbers.forEach(function(num) {
  console.log("Number:", num);
});

Loop Comparison Table

Loop Type Best Used For Condition Check
for When the number of iterations is known Before each iteration
while When iterations depend on a condition Before each iteration
do...while When code must run at least once After each iteration
for...of Iterating over arrays or strings N/A
for...in Iterating over object keys N/A
forEach Performing operations on each array element N/A

JavaScript Strings & Methods

Strings in JavaScript are sequences of characters used to represent text. You can create them using 'single quotes', "double quotes", or `backticks`. Backticks are useful for multi-line strings and embedding variables.

1. Creating Strings

Here are three ways to create a string in JavaScript:

// Example of creating strings
let str1 = 'Hello';
let str2 = "World";
let str3 = `Hello, ${str1} ${str2}`;
console.log(str3); // Output: Hello, Hello World

2. String Properties

.length → Returns the total number of characters in a string.

let text = "JavaScript";
console.log(text.length); // Output: 10

3. Case Conversion

Convert text to upper or lower case:

let name = "hello world";
console.log(name.toUpperCase()); // Output: HELLO WORLD
console.log(name.toLowerCase()); // Output: hello world

4. Searching Inside Strings

Find positions of text or check existence:

let text = "JavaScript is fun";
console.log(text.indexOf("Script")); // Output: 4
console.log(text.includes("fun"));    // Output: true

5. Extracting Parts of Strings

Use slice(), substring(), or substr() to extract parts of a string.

let text = "JavaScript";
console.log(text.slice(0, 4)); // Output: Java
console.log(text.substring(4, 10)); // Output: Script

6. Replacing Text

Replace specific parts of a string:

let text = "I love JavaScript";
console.log(text.replace("JavaScript", "Python"));
// Output: I love Python

let text2 = "JS is awesome. JS is fun!";
console.log(text2.replaceAll("JS", "JavaScript"));
// Output: JavaScript is awesome. JavaScript is fun!

7. Removing Extra Spaces

Clean unwanted spaces from the start and end of a string:

let text = "   Hello World   ";
console.log(text.trim());     // Output: Hello World
console.log(text.trimStart()); // Output: Hello World
console.log(text.trimEnd());   // Output: Hello World

8. Splitting and Joining Strings

let fruits = "Apple, Banana, Mango";
let arr = fruits.split(", ");
console.log(arr); // Output: ["Apple", "Banana", "Mango"]

let hello = "Hello";
let world = "World";
console.log(hello.concat(" ", world)); // Output: Hello World

9. Checking Start or End of a String

let text = "JavaScript";
console.log(text.startsWith("Java"));   // Output: true
console.log(text.endsWith("Script"));   // Output: true

10. Repeating Text

let text = "Hi! ";
console.log(text.repeat(3)); 
// Output: Hi! Hi! Hi!

11. Template Literals

Use backticks ` for embedding variables and multi-line strings:

let name = "Alice";
let age = 25;

let intro = `My name is ${name} and I am ${age} years old.`;
console.log(intro); 
// Output: My name is Alice and I am 25 years old.

JavaScript Arrays

Arrays are a fundamental data structure in JavaScript. They store multiple values in a single variable and provide powerful built-in methods for manipulation and iteration. Below, we'll cover everything from basic arrays to advanced iteration techniques, including 2D arrays.

1. What is an Array?

An array is an ordered collection of elements, indexed starting from 0. You can store numbers, strings, objects, or even other arrays. 

// Creating arrays
let numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4];
let mixed = ["Hello", 42, true, { name: "Alice" }];
let fruits = new Array("Apple", "Banana", "Mango");

console.log(numbers[0]); // 1
console.log(mixed[3].name); // Alice

2. Array Properties

The most commonly used property is length, which returns the number of elements in the array.

let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Mango"];
console.log(fruits.length); // 3

3. Common Array Methods

A) Adding & Removing Elements

  • push() - Add to the end
  • pop() - Remove from the end
  • unshift() - Add to the start
  • shift() - Remove from the start
let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana"];
fruits.push("Mango");
console.log(fruits); // ["Apple", "Banana", "Mango"]

fruits.pop();
console.log(fruits); // ["Apple", "Banana"]

B) Finding and Searching

  • indexOf() - Returns index of first match
  • lastIndexOf() - Returns index of last match
  • includes() - Checks if value exists
let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Mango"];
console.log(fruits.indexOf("Banana")); // 1
console.log(fruits.includes("Mango")); // true

C) Extracting & Combining

  • slice() - Extract part of an array (non-destructive)
  • splice() - Add or remove elements (modifies original array)
  • concat() - Merge arrays
let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Mango"];
let citrus = fruits.slice(1, 3);
console.log(citrus); // ["Banana", "Mango"]

4. Iteration Methods

Modern ways to iterate through arrays:

A) forEach()

let numbers = [1, 2, 3];
numbers.forEach(num => console.log(num));
// Output: 1, 2, 3

B) map()

let doubled = numbers.map(num => num * 2);
console.log(doubled); // [2, 4, 6]

C) filter()

let evens = numbers.filter(num => num % 2 === 0);
console.log(evens); // [2]

D) reduce()

let total = numbers.reduce((sum, num) => sum + num, 0);
console.log(total); // 6

E) for...of Loop

The for...of loop is a clean and simple way to iterate over array elements. 

let fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Mango"];
for (let fruit of fruits) {
  console.log(fruit);
}
// Output: Apple, Banana, Mango

5. Traditional Loops

A) for Loop

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  console.log(i);
}
// Output: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

B) while Loop

let i = 0;
while (i < 5) {
  console.log(i);
  i++;
}
// Output: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

C) do...while Loop

let j = 0;
do {
  console.log(j);
  j++;
} while (j < 5);
// Output: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Array Iteration

6. Two-Dimensional (2D) Arrays

A 2D array is an array of arrays, useful for grids, tables, and matrices. 

// Creating a 2D array
let matrix = [
  [1, 2, 3],
  [4, 5, 6],
  [7, 8, 9]
];

// Accessing elements
console.log(matrix[0][1]); // 2

// Iterating through a 2D array
for (let row of matrix) {
  for (let value of row) {
    console.log(value);
  }
}
// Output: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9

JavaScript Functions and Methods

Functions and methods are the heart of JavaScript programming. They allow us to write clean, reusable, and modular code that can solve complex problems efficiently.

1. What is a Function?

A function is a block of code designed to perform a specific task. It runs only when you call or invoke it. Functions are like recipes — you define the steps once, and you can execute them as many times as needed. 

// Basic Function
function greet() {
  console.log("Hello, welcome to JavaScript!");
}

greet(); // Output: Hello, welcome to JavaScript!

2. Why Use Functions?

  • To avoid writing the same code repeatedly.
  • To organize code into logical blocks.
  • To improve code reusability.
  • To make programs easier to test and debug.

3. Types of Functions

A) Function Declaration

Defined using the function keyword and can be called before or after it's declared because of hoisting.

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}
console.log(add(5, 3)); // Output: 8

B) Function Expression

Stored inside a variable. It is not hoisted, so it must be defined before calling.

const subtract = function(a, b) {
  return a - b;
};
console.log(subtract(10, 4)); // Output: 6

C) Arrow Function (ES6)

Shorter syntax introduced in ES6. Ideal for callbacks and concise code.

const multiply = (a, b) => a * b;
console.log(multiply(3, 4)); // Output: 12

D) Default Parameters

function greetUser(name = "Guest") {
  console.log("Hello, " + name);
}
greetUser(); // Hello, Guest
greetUser("Alice"); // Hello, Alice

E) Rest Parameters

Used when the number of arguments is unknown.

function sum(...nums) {
  return nums.reduce((total, num) => total + num, 0);
}
console.log(sum(1, 2, 3, 4)); // Output: 10
Function

4. Methods in JavaScript

A method is simply a function that belongs to an object.

const student = {
  name: "John",
  greet: function() {
    console.log("Hello, my name is " + this.name);
  }
};

student.greet(); // Output: Hello, my name is John

Real-World Example:

const calculator = {
  add: function(a, b) { return a + b; },
  subtract: function(a, b) { return a - b; },
  multiply: function(a, b) { return a * b; },
  divide: function(a, b) { return a / b; }
};

console.log(calculator.add(5, 3)); // 8

5. Common Built-in Methods

Category Method Example
String toUpperCase() "hello".toUpperCase() → HELLO
Array map() [1,2,3].map(x => x*2) → [2,4,6]
Object Object.keys() Object.keys({a:1, b:2}) → ["a", "b"]

Objects & JSON

What is an Object?

An object groups related data and actions in one place using key: value pairs. A function stored inside an object is called a method, and this inside a method means "the object it belongs to".

Run the code, then change it and run it again:

Looping Over Objects

MethodGives you
Object.keys(obj)Array of keys
Object.values(obj)Array of values
Object.entries(obj)Array of [key, value] pairs
for...inEach key (also inherited ones)

Use Object.entries with for...of (shown above) for the cleanest loop.

What is JSON?

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for sending data between a browser and a server. It looks like an object but follows stricter rules:

  • Keys must be in double quotes.
  • Strings must use double quotes (not single).
  • No functions, no undefined, no comments.
  • No trailing commas.
{
  "title": "JavaScript",
  "lessons": 16,
  "free": true,
  "tags": ["web", "beginner"]
}

Every time you use fetch and call response.json(), JavaScript is running JSON.parse for you.

Common Mistakes

  • Copying with =: const b = a does not copy, both names point to the same object.
  • Shallow copy: {...a} copies only the first level. Use structuredClone(a) for a full copy.
  • JSON.parse on bad text throws an error. Wrap it in try...catch (see the Error Handling lesson).

Scope, Hoisting & Closures

Scope: Where Can a Variable Be Seen?

Scope decides which parts of your code can use a variable.

ScopeCreated byVisible
GlobalDeclared outside everythingEverywhere
FunctionDeclared inside a functionOnly in that function
Blocklet / const inside { }Only inside that block

Inner code can see variables from outer scopes, but not the other way round.

This is why modern code prefers let and const over var.

Hoisting

Before running, JavaScript moves declarations to the top of their scope. This is called hoisting, and it behaves differently for each keyword:

DeclarationBefore the line runs
varExists, value is undefined
let / constExists but cannot be used (temporal dead zone) and throws an error
function declarationFully usable

Rule of thumb: declare variables at the top, before you use them.

Closures

A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the place where it was created, even after that outer function has finished.

Closures give you private data: nobody can touch count below except through the returned function.

• Used for counters, private state, event handlers and callbacks.
  • Each call to makeCounter() creates a new, separate closure.
  • The var loop surprise happens because all functions share one i.

Notes on Each Feature

  • Template literals use backticks and can hold any expression inside ${ }, and can span several lines.
  • Arrow functions are shorter, and they do not have their own this (they use the surrounding one). Use normal functions for object methods.
  • Destructuring pulls values out of arrays and objects into variables. You can rename ({ name: userName }) and set defaults ({ role = "student" }).
  • Spread (...) expands an array or object. Rest (...) collects the remaining items. Same symbol, opposite jobs.

Modules (a Preview)

Real projects split code into files and share it with export and import:

// math.js
export const add = (a, b) => a + b;
export default function multiply(a, b) { return a * b; }

// app.js
import multiply, { add } from "./math.js";
console.log(add(2, 3), multiply(2, 3));

You will use this constantly in the React part of the MERN stack.

Error Handling

Why Handle Errors?

Things go wrong: the user types bad data, the network drops, a file is missing. Without handling, one error stops your whole script. With try...catch you can react calmly and keep the app running.

try {
  // code that might fail
} catch (error) {
  // runs only if something above threw an error
} finally {
  // always runs (optional): cleanup
}

Throwing Your Own Errors

Use throw when your code detects a problem. Always throw an Error object (not a plain string) so you get a message and a stack trace. You can create your own error types by extending Error:

Common Error Types

TypeTypical cause
ReferenceErrorUsing a variable that does not exist
TypeErrorUsing a value in the wrong way (null.length, calling a non-function)
SyntaxErrorBroken code or bad JSON.parse text
RangeErrorA number outside the allowed range
ErrorThe general type, and the base of your own errors

Errors in Async Code

A try...catch also works with await, but it does not catch errors inside normal callbacks or setTimeout. With promises use .catch() or await inside try.

async function loadPosts() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch("/api/posts");
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Server said " + res.status);
    return await res.json();
  } catch (error) {
    console.log("Could not load posts:", error.message);
    return [];
  }
}

Good Habits

  • Catch errors where you can do something useful about them, not everywhere.
  • Never leave a catch block empty. At least log the error.
  • Show friendly messages to users and keep technical details in the console or logs.
  • Do not hide errors you did not expect: rethrow them (as in the example above).

Classes and Objects in JavaScript

In JavaScript, classes and objects are essential concepts for building structured, reusable, and organized code. Objects represent real-world entities, while classes act as blueprints for creating those objects. Let's explore them step by step with examples.

1. What is an Object?

An object in JavaScript is a collection of key-value pairs that store related data and functions (methods) together. 


const student = {
  name: "Ali",
  age: 20,
  course: "JavaScript",
  greet: function() {
    console.log(`Hello, my name is ${this.name} and I am learning ${this.course}`);
  }
};

console.log(student.name); // Output: Ali
student.greet(); // Output: Hello, my name is Ali and I am learning JavaScript
  • Properties: Variables inside the object (e.g., name, age).
  • Methods: Functions inside the object (e.g., greet()).
  • this: Refers to the current object.

2. What is a Class?

A class is like a blueprint for creating objects. It defines how an object should look and behave, but it doesn't hold data itself. Classes were introduced in ES6 for easier object-oriented programming. 


class ClassName {
  constructor() {
    // Initialize properties
  }

  methodName() {
    // Define methods
  }
}

3. Creating a Class and Object

Let's create a Student class and make objects from it.


class Student {
  constructor(name, age, course) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
    this.course = course;
  }

  greet() {
    console.log(`Hello, my name is ${this.name} and I am learning ${this.course}`);
  }
}

// Creating Objects
const student1 = new Student("Ali", 20, "JavaScript");
const student2 = new Student("Sara", 22, "Python");

student1.greet();
student2.greet();

4. Difference Between Class and Object

Feature Class Object
Definition A blueprint/template for creating objects A real instance created from a class
Purpose Defines properties and methods Stores actual data and behavior
Example class Student {} const s1 = new Student("Ali", 20)
Memory Usage Does not take memory until instantiated Takes memory because it stores actual values

5. Adding Methods in a Class

Methods are functions defined inside a class. There are two types: Instance Methods and Static Methods.

a) Instance Method


class Student {
  constructor(name) {
    this.name = name;
  }

  greet() {
    console.log(`Hello, ${this.name}`);
  }
}

const student = new Student("Ali");
student.greet();

b) Static Method

Static methods belong to the class itself, not to individual objects. 


class MathHelper {
  static add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
  }
}

console.log(MathHelper.add(5, 3)); // Output: 8

6. Inheritance in Classes

Inheritance allows a class to reuse properties and methods from another class using the extends keyword. 


class Person {
  constructor(name, age) {
    this.name = name;
    this.age = age;
  }

  greet() {
    console.log(`Hi, I'm ${this.name} and I am ${this.age} years old.`);
  }
}

class Student extends Person {
  constructor(name, age, course) {
    super(name, age); // Call parent constructor
    this.course = course;
  }

  study() {
    console.log(`${this.name} is studying ${this.course}`);
  }
}

const student = new Student("Sara", 22, "Python");
student.greet();
student.study();

7. Encapsulation (Private Properties)

JavaScript allows private properties using the # symbol. These properties cannot be accessed directly outside the class. 


class BankAccount {
  #balance = 0; // Private variable

  deposit(amount) {
    this.#balance += amount;
    console.log(`Deposited: $${amount}`);
  }

  getBalance() {
    return this.#balance;
  }
}

const account = new BankAccount();
account.deposit(500); // Deposited: $500
console.log(account.getBalance()); // 500
// console.log(account.#balance); ❌ Error: Private field cannot be accessed

8. Real-Life Example: Car Class


class Car {
  constructor(brand, model, year) {
    this.brand = brand;
    this.model = model;
    this.year = year;
  }

  start() {
    console.log(`${this.brand} ${this.model} is starting...`);
  }

  stop() {
    console.log(`${this.brand} ${this.model} has stopped.`);
  }
}

const car1 = new Car("Toyota", "Corolla", 2022);
car1.start();
car1.stop();

11. Why Use Classes?

  • Organized Code: Keeps related data and functions together.

Events in JavaScript

In JavaScript, events are actions or occurrences that happen in the browser or user interface. Events are how the browser lets you know that something happened, like when a user clicks a button, hovers over an element, presses a key, or submits a form. JavaScript can listen to these events and run specific code in response.

By using events, you can make your website interactive and dynamic. Think of events as “signals” that something has happened, and your JavaScript code can decide what to do when it hears these signals.

Common Types of Events

Event Type Description Examples
Mouse Events Triggered by mouse actions click, dblclick, mouseover, mouseout
Keyboard Events Triggered by keyboard actions keydown, keyup, keypress
Form Events Triggered when interacting with forms submit, change, input
Window Events Triggered by changes to the window or document load, resize, scroll

Events are handled using Event Listeners. The most common way to attach an event listener is by using the method: 

element.addEventListener("eventName", function() {
  // Code to run when event happens
});

1. Click Event

The click event is triggered when a user clicks on an element like a button or link. It is one of the most commonly used events in JavaScript. 

document.getElementById("clickBtn").addEventListener("click", function() {
  alert("Button was clicked!");
});

2. Mouse Events

Mouse events are triggered by interactions with the mouse, such as hovering, moving, or clicking. 

hoverBtn.addEventListener("mouseover", function() {
  console.log("Mouse is over the button!");
});
hoverBtn.addEventListener("mouseout", function() {
  console.log("Mouse left the button!");
});

3. Keyboard Events

Keyboard events are triggered when the user presses or releases a key on their keyboard. 

keyboardInput.addEventListener("keydown", function(event) {
  console.log("Key down: " + event.key);
});
keyboardInput.addEventListener("keyup", function(event) {
  console.log("Key up: " + event.key);
});

4. Prevent Default Action

The preventDefault() method stops the default behavior of an event from happening. For example, clicking on a link usually redirects to another page, but we can prevent that:

Go to Google 
googleLink.addEventListener("click", function(event) {
  event.preventDefault();
  alert("Link behavior stopped!");
});

5. Form Submission

Submitting a form usually reloads the page, but with preventDefault(), we can stop that behavior and handle the form with JavaScript instead. 

myForm.addEventListener("submit", function(event) {
  event.preventDefault();
  console.log("Form submitted!");
});

6. Event Delegation

Event delegation allows you to attach a single event listener to a parent element and handle events for its child elements.

  • Item A
  • Item B
  • Item C
list.addEventListener("click", function(event) {
  if(event.target.tagName === "LI") {
    alert("You clicked on " + event.target.textContent);
  }
});

7. Event Propagation (Bubbling & Capturing)

Event propagation determines how events move through the DOM hierarchy. There are two main phases:

  • Bubbling: The event starts from the innermost element and bubbles up to the parent.
  • Capturing: The event starts from the parent and goes down to the innermost element.
Outer Div
Inner Div 
outerDiv.addEventListener("click", function() {
  alert("Outer Div clicked!");
});

innerDiv.addEventListener("click", function(event) {
  alert("Inner Div clicked!");
  // event.stopPropagation(); // Uncomment to stop bubbling
});

JavaScript Event Listeners

An Event Listener in JavaScript allows you to listen for events on a specific HTML element and then run a piece of code whenever that event occurs.

Think of it like a doorbell system:

  • The event is someone pressing the doorbell button.
  • The event listener is you listening for the doorbell sound.
  • The callback function is what you do when you hear the sound, like opening the door.

Why Use Event Listeners?

Event listeners are better than inline event attributes like onclick="functionName()" for several reasons:

  1. Clean Code: Keeps your HTML and JavaScript separate.
  2. Multiple Events: You can attach more than one listener to the same element.
  3. Flexibility: You can add or remove listeners dynamically as needed.

Syntax of addEventListener()

element.addEventListener(event, callback, useCapture);
Parameter Description
event The type of event to listen for, such as "click", "mouseover", or "keydown".
callback The function that runs when the event happens.
useCapture (optional) A boolean value that determines the phase of event propagation:
false → Bubbling phase (default)
true → Capturing phase

Basic Example

Here is a simple example of a button click event:


document.getElementById("basicBtn").addEventListener("click", function() {
  document.getElementById("basicMsg").textContent = "Button was clicked!";
});

Example with a Named Function

Using a named function instead of an anonymous function makes your code easier to maintain:


function showMessage() {
  alert("Hello! You clicked the button!");
}

document.getElementById("namedBtn").addEventListener("click", showMessage);

Handling Multiple Events

You can attach multiple listeners to the same element, even for the same event type:
For this open the console screen


const btn = document.getElementById("multiBtn");

btn.addEventListener("click", function() {
  console.log("First action triggered");
});

btn.addEventListener("click", function() {
  console.log("Second action triggered");
});

Removing an Event Listener

You can remove an event listener, but you must use a named function so that JavaScript knows which function to remove. 


function greet() {
  console.log("Hello there!");
}

btn.addEventListener("click", greet);

// Later in the code:
btn.removeEventListener("click", greet);

The Event Object

When an event occurs, JavaScript automatically passes an event object to the callback function. This object contains details about the event such as:

  • Which key was pressed
  • Which mouse button was clicked
  • Which element triggered the event

btn.addEventListener("click", function(event) {
  console.log("Event type:", event.type);
  console.log("Target element:", event.target);
});

Practical Example: Click vs Double Click

Click or double-click the button below to see different actions:


const output = document.getElementById("output");
const actionBtn = document.getElementById("actionBtn");

actionBtn.addEventListener("click", function() {
  output.textContent = "You single clicked the button!";
});

actionBtn.addEventListener("dblclick", function() {
  output.textContent = "You double clicked the button!";
});

Inline Events vs Event Listeners

Inline Event Event Listener
<button onclick="sayHello()">Click</button> const btn = document.getElementById("btn");
btn.addEventListener("click", sayHello);
HTML and JavaScript are mixed together. HTML and JavaScript are separated, making it easier to maintain.

Summary

  • addEventListener() lets you listen for and respond to user actions.
  • You can attach multiple listeners to the same element.
  • Use named functions if you plan to remove listeners later.
  • The event object provides extra details about the event.
  • Separating HTML and JavaScript makes your code cleaner and easier to manage.

Web Storage

Saving Data in the Browser

Variables vanish when the page reloads. Web Storage lets you keep small pieces of data in the user's browser so they are still there next time. It stores only strings, as key/value pairs.

localStoragesessionStorageCookies
LastsUntil you delete itUntil the tab is closedUntil the expiry date
SizeAbout 5 MBAbout 5 MBAbout 4 KB
Sent to serverNoNoYes, with every request
Good forTheme, preferences, draftsOne-visit stateLogin sessions (set by the server)

The API

localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark");     // save
const theme = localStorage.getItem("theme"); // read -> "dark" (or null)
localStorage.removeItem("theme");            // delete one
localStorage.clear();                        // delete everything

sessionStorage has exactly the same methods. Try them in your browser console (press F12).

Storing Objects and Arrays

Because only strings can be stored, convert with JSON (see the Objects & JSON lesson):

const settings = { theme: "dark", fontSize: 18 };
localStorage.setItem("settings", JSON.stringify(settings));

const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("settings")) || { theme: "light", fontSize: 16 };
console.log(saved.theme);

Example: A Draft That Survives Reload

const box = document.querySelector("#note");

box.value = localStorage.getItem("draft") || "";   // restore on page load

box.addEventListener("input", () => {
  localStorage.setItem("draft", box.value);         // save on every change
});

This is the same idea Learning Hub uses to keep your work safe if you close the tab.

Security Rules

  • Never store passwords or secret tokens in localStorage. Any script on the page (for example through an XSS bug) can read it.
  • Never trust stored data: users can edit it in the browser. Always validate on the server.
  • Wrap JSON.parse in try...catch because the stored text might be damaged.
  • This is why Learning Hub keeps your login in a secure, HttpOnly cookie and only a short-lived token in memory.

JavaScript Asynchronous Concepts

Learn how JavaScript handles asynchronous operations using callbacks, promises, and async/await.

1. Callback Functions

A callback function is a function passed to another function and executed later.

// Callback Example
function greet(name, callback) {
  console.log("Hello " + name);
  callback();
}

function sayGoodbye() {
  console.log("Goodbye!");
}

greet("Alice", sayGoodbye);

2. Callback Hell

Nested callbacks can make code messy and hard to maintain.

doSomething(function(result) {
  doSomethingElse(result, function(newResult) {
    doAnotherThing(newResult, function(finalResult) {
      console.log("Final result: " + finalResult);
    });
  });
});

3. Promises

A Promise represents the eventual result (success or failure) of an async operation.

let myPromise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  let success = true;
  if(success) resolve("Task completed!");
  else reject("Task failed!");
});

myPromise.then(result => console.log(result))
         .catch(error => console.log(error));

4. Promise Chaining

Use .then() multiple times to chain async tasks sequentially.

new Promise((resolve) => resolve(5))
.then(result => result * 2)
.then(result => result + 3)
.then(result => console.log(result)); // 13

5. Async/Await

Write asynchronous code like synchronous code using async and await.

function fetchData() {
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve("Data received!"), 2000));
}

async function getData() {
  const result = await fetchData();
  console.log(result);
}

getData();

6. Which is Better?

Feature Callback Promise Async/Await
Readability Poor Good Excellent
Error Handling Difficult Easy Very Easy
Maintenance Hard Medium Easy
Sequential Calls Messy Easy Very Easy

Fetch API in JavaScript

The Fetch API is a modern way to make network requests in JavaScript. It is simpler, cleaner, and uses Promises, making it easier to handle asynchronous code compared to the older XMLHttpRequest.

1. What is Fetch API?

The Fetch API lets you send and receive data asynchronously between a browser and a server. You can use it to:

  • Fetch data from APIs.
  • Send data to a server.
  • Work with JSON, text, images, and more.

2. Why Use Fetch API?

Feature XMLHttpRequest (Old Way) Fetch API (Modern Way)
Syntax Complex and verbose Clean and readable
Returns Callbacks Promises
JSON Handling Manual parsing required Built-in .json()
Error Handling Messy Simple with .catch()

3. Basic Syntax

fetch(url, options)
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.error('Error:', error));

4. Making a Simple GET Request

fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log("Fetched Data:", data))
  .catch(error => console.error("Error fetching data:", error));

5. Making a POST Request

fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json'
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    title: 'My New Post',
    body: 'This is the content of the post',
    userId: 1
  })
})
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(data => console.log("Post created:", data))
  .catch(error => console.error("Error creating post:", error));

6. Handling HTTP Errors

fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/invalid-url')
  .then(response => {
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error('HTTP Error! Status: ' + response.status);
    }
    return response.json();
  })
  .then(data => console.log("Data received:", data))
  .catch(error => console.error("Error occurred:", error.message));

7. Using Fetch with Async/Await

async function fetchPost() {
  try {
    let response = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1');
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error('HTTP Error: ' + response.status);
    }
    let data = await response.json();
    console.log("Fetched using async/await:", data);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Fetch failed:", error);
  }
}
fetchPost();

8. Displaying Data in HTML

Example: Fetch the first 5 posts and display them as a list.

fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?_limit=5')
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(posts => {
    const list = document.getElementById('post-list');
    posts.forEach(post => {
      const li = document.createElement('li');
      li.textContent = post.title;
      list.appendChild(li);
    });
  })
  .catch(error => console.error("Error:", error));

    9. Best Practices with Fetch

    • Always check response.ok to handle HTTP errors.
    • Use async/await for cleaner code.
    • Always handle network failures with .catch().
    • Keep API URLs and keys in separate config files.
    • Use try...catch for better error handling.
